title: WNBA faces transgender eligibility row after Cunningham comments
dek: Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's statements opposing transgender women in sports have triggered national political attention and exposed ambiguity in the WNBA's eligibility rules. Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom has declared intent to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft, testing whether the league's definition of 'women' will be enforced.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The WNBA collective bargaining agreement states 'Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA,' but does not define what constitutes being a woman.
bottom_line: Watch for the WNBA's formal response at the commissioner's meeting with team presidents, and whether the league clarifies what definition of "woman" it will apply to eligibility decisions. The story's trajectory hinges on whether the WNBA, through its collective bargaining process, articulates or maintains a definition, and whether Kanter Freedom or others file formal applications that force the rule's enforcement.
body: Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham told ESPN last month that she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport, according to BBC Sport. The 29-year-old, in her eighth WNBA season, later doubled down on those remarks, saying it was "common sense" to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.

Cunningham's statements have drawn criticism from those who believed she "hated" transgender people, a charge she denied. She later said she is "not a very political person." President Donald Trump expressed support for her position, and Vice President JD Vance called her "inspiring," per BBC Sport. Competing rallies from critics and supporters have been organized at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.

The row has exposed an ambiguity in the WNBA's eligibility framework. The league's collective bargaining agreement, negotiated between the WNBA and its players association, states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," according to BBC Sport. The agreement does not, however, define what constitutes being a woman. No openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA, making the debate prospective rather than responsive to an actual case.

WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week stating the matter would be discussed at an upcoming meeting with team presidents. In the memo, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league," per BBC Sport. She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."

Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022 and played 11 seasons in the league, declared on Instagram: "I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect." He wrote: "If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA." Kanter Freedom, known for speaking out on human rights issues, stated: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices." According to BBC Sport, the WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's remarks.
